bib.title: Challenges in Deploying Machine Learning: a Survey of Case Studies

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Challenges in Deploying Machine Learning: a Survey of Case Studies", Andrei Paleyes (Cambridge), Raoul-Gabriel Urma (Cambridge Spark), Neil D. Lawrence (Cambridge). arXiv:2011.09926v3 [cs.LG], 19 May 2022. Venue CONFIRMED in the PDF: "ACM Comput. Surv., Vol. 1, No. 1, Article 1 (January 2022), 29 pages. https://doi.org/10.1145/3533378" (ISSN 0360-0300). The 2020 in the filename is the arXiv v1 date; cite as ACM Computing Surveys 2022.

COVERAGE: all 29 pages read; about 122,600 of 122,626 chars of body text (main text through Conclusion, about 1,000 lines). The reference list (about 160 entries) was skimmed only for origins. A fontTools warning appeared at extraction. It affects math glyphs only. Text is otherwise clean, with odd mid-word spaces and ligature artifacts, so quotes below keep those.

STAGE TAXONOMY (Table 1, p.3-4). The workflow follows Ashmore et al. [14], with four stages. The paper stresses these are "not as a timeline" because the stages run in parallel and feed back into each other. Requirements formulation is out of scope. The paper chose this scheme over CRISP-DM or TDSP because it "defines a larger number of deployment steps".
1. Data management. Steps: collection (data discovery), preprocessing (data dispersion, cleaning), augmentation (labeling of large volumes, access to experts, lack of high-variance data), analysis (data profiling).
2. Model learning. Steps: model selection (complexity, resource-constrained environments, interpretability), training (computational cost, environmental impact, privacy-aware training), hyper-parameter selection (resource-heavy techniques, unknown search space, hardware-aware optimization).
3. Model verification. Steps: requirement encoding (performance metrics, business-driven metrics), formal verification (regulatory frameworks), test-based verification (simulation-based testing, data validation routines, edge case testing).
4. Model deployment. Steps: integration (operational support, reuse of code and models, software engineering anti-patterns, mixed team dynamics), monitoring (feedback loops, outlier detection, custom design tooling), updating (concept drift, continuous delivery).
Cross-cutting: ethics (aggravation of biases, fairness and accountability, authorship, decision making); law (country-level regulations, abiding by existing legislation, focus on technical solution only); end users' trust (involvement of end users, user experience, explainability score); security (data poisoning, model stealing, model inversion).
The paper does NOT rank challenges by severity.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Central claim: practitioners face challenges at every stage of the deployment workflow, which the paper stresses over any single dominant failure point.
  number: none
  setup: literature survey of published case studies, review papers and "lessons learned" papers, last five years, with few exceptions. No interviews.
  quote: "The main contribution of our paper is to show that practitioners face challenges at each stage of the machine learning deployment workflow."
  where: p.2

- Model changes on three axes, so continuous delivery for ML is harder than for ordinary software.
  number: three axes (code, model, data)
  setup: conceptual, via Sato et al. [63]
  quote: "CD for machine learning solutions is complicated because, unlike in regular software products where changes only happen in the code, ML solutions experience change along three axes: the code, the model and the data."
  where: p.13

- Better model metrics did not give business value at scale.
  number: 150 models
  setup: Booking.com [62]. Proxy metrics such as clicks failed to convert to business metrics such as conversion.
  quote: "an increase in model performance does not translate into a gain in business value, as Booking.com discovered after deploying 150 models into production [62]"
  where: p.10
  (The quote has no "t" in "translate" in the raw text due to spacing. Verify against the PDF if quoting exactly.)

- Business metrics should also drive monitoring and update quality control.
  number: none
  quote: "Once defined, these metrics should also be used for monitoring the production environment and for quality control of model updates."
  where: p.10

- Start with a simple model to get the deployment pipeline in place.
  number: single hidden layer, 32 ReLU units
  setup: Airbnb search [39]. The team abandoned a complex deep model after failed deployments. The pipeline built for the simple model was the benefit.
  quote: "a single hidden layer NN with 32 fully connected ReLU activations. Even such a simple model had value, as it allowed the building of a whole pipeline of deploying ML models in a production setting"
  where: p.7

- Deployment time and failure rates from industry surveys (secondhand, not the authors' data).
  number: 8 to 90 days; 18%; 2,473 organizations
  setup: Algorithmia reports [5, 6]; IDC [7]
  quote: "the majority of companies reporting between 8 and 90 days to deploy a single model, and 18% taking even more time. A report by IDC [7] surveyed 2,473 organizations and found that a significant portion of their attempted AI deployments fail"
  where: p.2

- Monitoring is an open problem, and off-the-shelf tooling often does not fit.
  number: none
  setup: Sculley et al. [71] on monitoring and feedback loops. Ackermann et al. [73] on an early intervention system for two US police departments, which had to build integrity checks, top-k change metrics and rank-correlation anomaly tracking from scratch.
  quote: "Monitoring of evolving input data, prediction bias and overall performance of ML models is an open problem."
  where: p.13

- Concept drift remains critical, and drift detection links to monitoring.
  number: none
  setup: defined as changes in the joint distribution p(X, y). Can be discrete or gradual.
  quote: "Even though concept drift has been known for decades [81], these examples show that it remains a critical problem for applications of ML today."
  where: p.14

- Data validation must sit in the pipeline.
  number: none
  setup: Breck et al. [68]. Problems arise when data generation is decoupled from the ML pipeline.
  quote: "it is imperative to catch them early by including data validation routines in the ML pipeline."
  where: p.11

- Research and engineering should share one codebase.
  number: none
  setup: Amershi et al. [12]
  quote: "it is beneficial to include researchers in the whole development journey, making sure they own the product codebase along with the engineers, use the same version control and participate in code reviews."
  where: p.12

- Reuse of embeddings simplified pipelines.
  number: three models
  setup: Pinterest [70]
  quote: "There are three models used in Pinterest internally which use similar embeddings, and initially they were maintained completely separately"
  where: p.12

- ML-specific technical debt anti-patterns (Sculley et al. [71]): abstraction boundary erosion, correction cascades, glue code, pipeline jungles, configuration debt.
  number: none
  quote: "Some of these issues, such as abstraction boundary erosion and correction cascades" ... "Others, such as glue code or pipeline jungles"
  where: p.12

- Training cost.
  number: $50k to $1.6m
  setup: BERT full training in cloud compute, per Sharir et al. [46], depending on model size
  quote: "full training procedure can cost anywhere between $50k and $1.6m in cloud computing resources"
  where: p.8

- Environmental cost.
  number: four cars' lifetime CO2 per NAS training cycle
  setup: Strubell et al. [49]
  quote: "one full training cycle utilizing neural architecture search emits an amount of CO2 comparable to what four average cars emit in their whole life time"
  where: p.9

- Membership inference accuracy.
  number: 70% to 94%
  setup: Shokri et al., against models trained on ML-as-a-service providers
  quote: "achieving anywhere from 70% up to 94% accuracy of membership inference"
  where: p.9

- Data poisoning and model stealing figures (security).
  number: 8% poisoning rate; half of patients; 650 to 4013 queries; 70s to 2088s; 16 hours
  setup: Jagielski et al. [119] on a linear model for medical dosage. Tramèr et al. [121] on Google, Amazon and Microsoft ML services. Microsoft Tay bot.
  quote: "malicious samples with an 8% poisoning rate in the training set resulted in incorrect dosage for half of the patients" / "the number of queries ranging from 650 to 4013 to extract an equivalent model and in time ranging from 70s to 2088s" / "Within 16 hours of its release a troubling percentage of Tay's messages were abusive or offensive"
  where: p.18

- Labeling at scale is hard.
  number: up to about 100% label error; 1.5 million packets/s
  setup: network traffic classification, per Pacheco et al. [28] and a cited study [29]
  quote: "existing tools for label assignment can introduce errors into collected ML datasets of network traffic data, going as high as almost 100% for certain applications"
  where: p.6

- Simulation-based testing is not a full replacement for real-world testing.
  number: none
  setup: autonomous vehicles [35]. RL cognitive engine on the ISS [67], where only a subset of planned experiments could be run despite ground testing.
  quote: "simulation-based testing hinges on assumptions made by simulation developers, and therefore cannot be considered a full replacement for real-world testing."
  where: p.11

- Formal verification rarely happens. Quality is set through regulation instead (banking model risk guidance from the UK PRA and ECB).
  number: none
  quote: "such verification could include mathematical proofs of correctness or numerical estimates of output error bounds, but as Ashmore et. al. [14] point out this rarely happens in practice."
  where: p.10

- Model updates can be backward incompatible and hurt human-AI team performance.
  number: none
  setup: Bansal et al. [85], Srivastava et al. [86]
  quote: "updating an AI model to increase accuracy, at the expense of compatibility, may degrade overall AI-human team performance."
  where: p.14
  (Raw text reads "Authors proceeded to show that updating an AI model to increase accuracy, at the expense of compatibility, may degrade overall AI-Human team performance". Use the raw wording if quoting.)

- Holistic remedies are costly to adopt.
  number: none
  setup: Section 8.2 lists datasheets for datasets, DVC, model cards, Data Oriented Architectures, MLTRL (Lavin et al. [157]), and Zinkevich's Google best-practices rules [158]
  quote: "all such approaches assume significant time investment, because they represent significant changes to current norms in project management and development."
  where: p.21

- Tools add dependencies. Section 8.1 names SageMaker, Microsoft ML, Uber Michelangelo, TFX and MLflow for operational maintenance. Jenga, CheckList and Data Linter are named for quality assurance. Snorkel, Snuba and cleanlab are named for weak supervision. Auto-keras, Auto-sklearn and TPOT are named for AutoML. Alibi Detect is named for drift.
  number: none
  quote: "by using a particular tool they introduce an additional dependency into their solution. While a single additional dependency seems manageable, their number can quickly grow and become a maintenance burden."
  where: p.19

LIMITS
- This is a literature survey, not a measurement. It has no systematic search protocol, no counts of how often each challenge is reported, and no ranking. Quote: "we do not attempt to prioritize the challenges".
- No interviews were done. The authors list interviews and a comparative analysis across industries as future work.
- Non-technical challenges are not covered. The authors call the set of challenges "far from complete".
- Infrastructure and storage (databases, query engines), requirements formulation and general security (access control, code vulnerabilities) are explicitly out of scope.
- The authors note a "relative shortage of deployment experience reports in the academic literature", so the evidence base is skewed toward what gets published.
- It is not a maturity model. It has no levels or scoring. MLOps is mentioned only in a footnote (p.11, which uses "AIOps" following Dang et al. [69]). It gives no measured effect of any practice.
- Dated: the tool list (2020-2021) predates LLM and foundation-model deployment. Cost figures are from the BERT era.
- Many numbers are secondhand from cited studies, with their own setups.

BUILDS ON
- Ashmore et al. [14] for the four-stage workflow. CRISP-DM [15] and TDSP [16] are named as alternatives.
- Sculley et al. [71] (technical debt) for monitoring and anti-patterns.
- Breck et al. [68] for data validation.
- Amershi et al. [12] for software engineering in ML.
- Baier et al. [13] is the only general-purpose prior survey they found, IT-sector focused.
- Lavin et al. [157] for MLTRL.
- Zinkevich [158] for Google's rules of ML.
- Gebru et al. [151] for datasheets.
- Mitchell et al. [153] for model cards.
- Dang et al. [69] for AIOps.
- Lawrence [150] for data readiness levels.
(Entry numbers are as printed in the paper. Years were not checked in the reference list.)

CODE: none (no code in the paper).

FIGURES: none extracted. Table 1 on p.3-4 is the key artifact (stage, step and issue map, reproduced in the taxonomy above).

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Extraction has mid-word spaces and ligatures (for example "deploy ment", "ﬁ", "ﬂ"), so verbatim quotes may need cleaning before use. The "translate" quote in the Booking.com claim has a spacing glitch. The Bansal quote is flagged above. Page numbers are the ACM article page (1:N), not the PDF page, though the two are the same here (29 pages).
